Long [aː] plus [r], the stressed vowel that gives the name its meaning: "vow, agreement".

pronunciation.approximation: 'VAHR' — one long syllable, the vowel held like the 'a' in 'father' and ending with a light rolled 'r'.

domains.title: The Vow
domains.subtitle: Goddess of Betrothals and Marriage Agreements
domains.lead: Vár is the goddess who hears the vows that bind. Her name is the Old Norse word for "pledge" or "betrothal," and she is invoked whenever men and women make marriage agreements. In Snorri's catalogue she is one of the Ásynjur, the divine witness to contracts of the heart and the household.

cards.name: Witness of Vows
cards.desc: She is the goddess who hears and remembers every pledge made between lovers and kin.

cards.name: Marriage Agreement
cards.desc: Marriages were made in her name; to break a vow sworn to Vár was to invite her judgment.

cards.name: Husbands' Oaths
cards.desc: Snorri says that women call upon Vár in matters of betrothal and the oaths between husbands and wives.

cards.name: Sacred Bond
cards.desc: She guards the agreement that turns two households into one, the spoken contract at the heart of marriage.

symbols.name: Joined hands

mythology.lead: Vár's mythology is concentrated in a single paragraph of Snorri, but her importance is social: she is the divine sanction behind marriage.

myths.title: Goddess of Betrothal
myths.text: Snorri writes: "The ninth is Vár. She hears the oaths and private agreements that men and women make with each other. Therefore these oaths are called várar. She also punishes those who break them." With that single sentence she becomes the divine witness to the most consequential contract in human life.

myths.title: Oaths Called Várar
myths.text: The Old Norse word vár, "pledge, betrothal," gives its name to a class of oaths. A vow sworn "á Várar hendr" — into Vár's hands — was a solemn undertaking, especially in marriage and inheritance. The goddess is thus embedded in the legal language of the North, her name invoked whenever honor and contract meet.

myths.title: Among the Goddesses of Order
myths.text: Vár appears in the þulur and in Snorri's list as one of the Ásynjur who oversee the orderly life of gods and humans. Alongside Vǫr (the knowing one) and Sága (the seeing one), she belongs to the divine bureaucracy that keeps words and bonds sacred.

lore.syncretism: Vár is the Norse counterpart to several oath- and marriage-goddesses. The Greek Hera presides over lawful marriage; the Roman Juno is invoked in weddings as Juno Pronuba; the Germanic Tīw gives his name to Tuesday and to the thing, the assembly where oaths were sworn. Within Norse tradition, Vár is distinct from Frigg (the queenly wife) and Freyja (the goddess of desire): she is the contract itself, the spoken promise that makes marriage a matter of public honor rather than private passion.
lore.culturalLegacy: Vár survives in the Scandinavian and Germanic legal vocabulary of vows and in modern Heathen wedding ceremonies, where she is sometimes invoked as witness. Her name is less common in popular retellings than those of Freyja or Frigg, but her function remains central: every wedding is, in some sense, made before Vár. Restoring Vár preserves the long vowel and acute accent that mark the name as the Old Norse word for the pledge itself.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Vár is the goddess who takes words seriously. In a world where oaths were binding not because of a court but because of honor, she was the divine reminder that speech creates obligation. A vow spoken in her name could not be casually broken; to do so was to insult the goddess and the community that trusted her.

Her meditation is the meditation of integrity. She asks: what have you promised, and have you kept your word? Not all vows should be kept — some are extracted by force or made in ignorance — but the habit of keeping one's word is the foundation of trust. Vár is the goddess of that foundation.

lore.archaeology: Vár is a purely textual figure. No runestone, image, or place-name is securely hers. Her presence is in the legal vocabulary of Old Norse and in the manuscript tradition of Snorri's Prose Edda.
